item.title: The machines that keep America alive are failing. We forgot how to replace them
item.description: U.S. electricity demand surged 7% since 2020, but two decades of disinvestment hollowed out the workforce and supply chain needed to meet it.
item.content:encoded:
For 20 years, electricity was the most boring business in America, and our industry built its whole infrastructure strategy around the assumption that things would stay that way.

The numbers tell the story. From 2010 to 2020, U.S. electricity consumption fell by roughly 1%. LEDs, efficient motors and tightening appliance standards quietly cancelled out the electricity used by every new subdivision, factory and data hall, and then some. Demand was flat, and planners treated this as a permanent fact of life rather than as what it actually was: an intermission.

No-growth industries make choices that are perfectly rational, yet corrosive. You don't fund apprenticeships when there's no new capacity to staff. You don't keep spare metallurgical know-how on the payroll when nobody's ordering. You don't recruit ambitious 25-year-olds into a sector whose pitch is "stable, essential, and never going anywhere."

TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT EFFECTIVELY PAUSES NEW DATA CENTER PROJECTS PENDING STATEWIDE GRID AUDIT

So, the utilities didn't. The transformer makers didn't. The steel mills didn't. The workforce aged in place and the labor pipeline behind it ran dry.

We mistook a flat line for stability and in doing so, allowed a slow decay to occur. Then the line broke.

Since 2020, electricity consumption has reversed two decades of decline and climbed about 7%. Demand for large power transformers, the equipment through which nearly all of America's electricity passes at some point, has surged 116% since 2019. Data centers, reshoring, electrification and grid hardening all arrived in the same handful of years, descending on an industry that had bought into the idea that it would never grow again.

Facing resurgent demand, we went looking for the people and the parts to meet resurgent demand, and here is what we found: America had forgotten how to make pipes.

TRUMP’S REINDUSTRIALIZATION AGENDA FACES ITS BIGGEST HURDLE — AMERICANS

Roughly 80% of the large power transformers the United States installs are now imported. The grain-oriented electrical steel at the heart of every one of them has but a single domestic producer. Lead times for a standard power transformer have stretched to nearly two and a half years, and the larger units that connect power plants to the grid run longer still. Prices are up more than 77% since 2019. The average transformer already humming away on the American grid is 38 years old, and more than 70% of the fleet is past age 25.

We are simultaneously trying to replace an aging base and build an entirely new one with a supply chain we spent a generation hollowing out.

The hardware shortage gets the headlines. The human one is worse, because you can't expedite it. A person cannot, today, enroll anywhere in America to learn how to design or build a large power transformer. The handful of university power-engineering programs that survived the last two decades don't teach it. They were shrinking before the boom began as students chased software and AI instead.

The knowledge to wind a coil, design a core or run a high-voltage acceptance test is tribal, passed hand-to-hand on a shop floor by master winders, test engineers or metallurgists who understand why a core behaves the way it does. The expertise lives in people, much of it never written down, and roughly half the utility workforce is now over 45 with a large share eligible to retire this decade.

You can stand up a new transformer factory in a couple of years. You cannot conjure an experienced winder in a couple of years, and you can't enroll one either.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That's the asymmetry nobody priced in. Industrial capability is cheap to lose and brutally expensive to rebuild. It took just 18 months of supply chain stress to expose the gap. It will take the better part of two decades to close it — and that's the optimistic case where demand politely waits. It won't. Every credible forecast has load climbing through 2050.

OUR ENEMIES FOUND A WEAKNESS IN ESSENTIAL TECHNOLOGY. WE MUST FIX IT … FAST

We've finally admitted that electricity is as essential as water, but we did so too late to avoid disruption. The fix is slow and unglamorous.

It means treating the grid as a growth industry again, which means apprenticeships, demand signals long enough for manufacturers to justify new lines, and a domestic materials base that isn't one bad quarter at one steel plant away from seizing up. It means capital flowing to electrical capacity, not just to the data centers that capacity will serve.

Most of all, it means abandoning the belief that quietly governed 20 years of disinvestment: that because the lights stayed on, the people and the plants that keep them on would always be there. The bill for two decades of treating an intermission as the end of the show has come due all at once.

item.title: AI has an opinion and it usually leans left. You have a right to know its agenda
item.description: Trump's AI Action Plan demands models pursue objective truth, as research reveals undisclosed left-leaning biases that could influence voters at scale.
item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence sits at the center of nearly every major debate, from jobs and data centers to healthcare, national security and consumer protection. Missing from the national spotlight, however, is a more fundamental question: Will AI models pursue the truth, or will they be permitted to bury undisclosed biases inside their responses? 

On the surface, general-purpose AI tools present themselves as neutral sources of information and analysis, capable of answering most questions with citations, well-reasoned explanations and unbiased feedback. 

But reality paints a different picture. While it is easy to spot and dismiss the most egregious violations of neutrality and accuracy (e.g., depictions of the Founding Fathers as African American or British medieval kings as racially diverse), underlying biases are not as readily apparent. The average user is much less likely to detect when a model is steering them toward an engineered outcome or framing a response through a politically skewed lens, as data shows most users do not fact-check answers from AI models.

Reporting and research are beginning to shine a light on the existence of these undisclosed biases. The Washington Post, for instance, tested the leading models on hot-button political questions and found that they consistently favored left-leaning arguments while presenting those positions as neutral. 

AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’

MIT’s Center for Constructive Communication reached similar conclusions, documenting that reward models display left-leaning biases even when trained on truthful statements, with strong bias on topics like climate, energy and labor unions. 

At the state level, ambitious lawmakers are exploiting the absence of federal preemption to pursue codifying these hidden biases. In New York and California, legislators are seeking to advance bills akin to Colorado’s original Artificial Intelligence Act, which would impose impact assessments and anti-discrimination mandates. 

As proposed, these frameworks would create structural incentives for companies to alter or omit information from responses to avoid legal liability. The FTC’s own reading of Colorado’s AI law is that it "appears to coerce companies into altering the output of their AI models" to advance the state’s ideological objectives. In other words, politicians are attempting to enact laws that, in practice, penalize accurate model responses. 

These biases are not trivial or immaterial. AI is being adopted at a scale faster than any technology in history. Millions of Americans rely on it to find information, complete their work and seek advice. Many are even using it to make sense of our current political environment. 

FOX NEWS POLL: MOVE OVER BIG BROTHER, VOTERS SEE BIG TECH AS GREATER THREAT TO US

A recent New York Times report highlighted how voters are increasingly using AI chatbots to determine which candidate to support. The Times noted, "Voters are turning to new AI tools to serve as nonpartisan researchers, viewing them as a viable alternative to traditional news coverage, voter guides or social media."

While these systems can make political engagement more accessible, a model’s undisclosed ideological leanings can filter information through a biased lens and generate a seemingly neutral answer that is capable of shifting voter opinion on a candidate or policy topic.

At scale, these hidden biases cease to be a harmless quirk or unintended outcome. Instead, they become capable of materially influencing matters central to Americans’ personal, professional, and civic life. 

Enter President Donald Trump. Under his leadership, the Trump administration is actively confronting these concerns. The historic AI Action Plan made clear that American AI must be trustworthy and "designed to pursue objective truth rather than social engineering agendas when users seek factual information or analysis." Subsequent executive orders also blocked federal procurement of biased AI models and ensured that model accuracy is governed under a federal framework. 

Pursuant to the order that created a national AI framework, FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson issued a proposed policy statement applying existing consumer protection law to undisclosed model bias. 

As the FTC outlines, under Section 5 of the FTC Act, a representation or omission is deceptive if it is likely to mislead a reasonable consumer and is material to that consumer’s decisions. An AI system presented as a neutral source of information while systematically laundering preferred narratives under the guise of objectivity would meet that threshold. 

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Ferguson’s policy proposal also reasserts federal jurisdiction. AI models are standardized products designed for nationwide sale, not localized adaptations. However, the current 50-state patchwork allows the most aggressive state legislatures to effectively set the national standard, as complying with the most burdensome regime becomes the most cost-effective. The FTC’s solution applies a single federal standard for AI models that is no different from the way we already regulate products sold nationally, like automobiles and pharmaceuticals.

This is a commonsense proposal: if a model carries a hidden bias or steers a user contrary to his reasonable expectations, then such alterations must be clearly disclosed to the user, or models risk violating federal consumer protection law. 

The American people have a right to know if they are being deceived. The FTC’s proposed policy statement is a necessary step toward fulfilling the mission laid out in the AI Action Plan and advancing American leadership in the AI age.

item.title: Democratic group launches $15M war on DSA after socialist primary wins: 'Mortal danger'
item.description: Third Way launches $15 million campaign against Democratic Socialists of America, calling the DSA a "mortal danger" after Michigan's primary.
item.content:encoded:
A leading centrist Democratic group is launching a new $15 million effort between now and 2028 to discredit democratic socialism, Fox News Digital confirms.

The group, Third Way, says it plans to target the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which they believe poses a "mortal danger" for Democrats.

The move comes in the wake of left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s victory this week over more moderate Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens in the high-profile and high-stakes Senate primary in battleground Michigan.

El-Sayed's razor-thin win over Stevens, along with DSA-aligned and progressive candidates winning in two congressional primaries in Michigan, come amid earlier victories this spring and earlier this summer, and are emboldening the left in its ideological battle for the future of the Democratic Party.

MEET THE FAR LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS

"We believe the DSA poses a serious threat to Democrats. Their ideas are dangerous and their politics are toxic. If we are to beat MAGA Republicans, we cannot allow our party to be defined by radicals," Third Way co-founder Matt Bennett told Fox News Digital.

The group says their effort will include opposition research into the DSA, polling, social media programs and educating Democratic activists and leaders, but that their push is not directed at individual candidates, some of whom are now the party's nominees in a growing number of congressional races in this year's midterm elections.

Responding, DSA co-chair Megan Romer told Fox News Digital, "$15 million to tell working class people that a better world isn’t possible? We believe in people power, and our vision for a better future is winning. We will keep building our movement, and they will waste their money."

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

A growing concern among moderate Democrats is that nominating far-left candidates in key Senate and House races could endanger the party's midterm effort to win back congressional majorities from the Republicans.

They're also concerned that this year's primary victories by the left-wing at the expense of establishment-backed incumbents and candidates could boost progressive contenders in the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination race, which will get underway after November's elections.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Referring to El-Sayed's victory in Michigan, which is an early voting state in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary calendar, Bennett said it "gives the 2028 presidential field the wrong idea of how to win the presidential primary in places in Michigan."

News of the Third Way effort was first reported earlier Thursday by the New York Times.

item.title: Fauci's contempt of Congress is challengeable, but not his contempt for the public
item.description: The Senate contempt vote against Anthony Fauci raises complex legal questions about whether his Fifth Amendment claims hold up against Biden's pardon.
item.content:encoded:
"Today I am the most famous and talked-about person in the country." Those words from the diary of Dr. Anthony Fauci are certainly true as the U.S. Senate Committee on Homeland Security & Governmental Affairs moves forward with holding him in contempt for refusing to answer over a hundred questions about his past conduct and statements as the former head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

The contempt vote will start a process that is fraught with political and legal challenges. Even putting aside the objections to the direct referral from the Committee to the Justice Department (rather than submit the matter to a full Senate vote), there remain serious questions about whether Fauci can be held in contempt after invoking his right to remain silent under the Fifth Amendment. As I have previously stated, this area is rather murky and Fauci likely has the advantage in any litigation.

At the outset, it is important to note that Fauci always faced a risk of perjury in his prior appearances. Even if immunized, a witness can always be prosecuted for false statements. Fauci is in a much stronger position today than he was in prior hearings due to the sweeping pardon he received from former President Joe Biden. Yet, he suddenly decided to remain silent when his own words came back to contradict him.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Now for the legal questions.

If a witness is immunized, they can be compelled to testify. If, for example, the Senate granted Fauci immunity, there would be little question about his answering these questions as well as the ability to charge him for any false statements.

The Senate Committee is arguing that the Biden pardon had the same impact. Since Fauci cannot be prosecuted for any acts during the extended period of the pardon (going back to 2014 when the government allegedly funded "gain-of-function research). Chairman Rand Paul did an excellent job in putting this issue into sharp relief in his final set of questions by framing his inquiry as confined to the period of his pardon.

The argument is credible and, for many, compelling: since Fauci cannot be prosecuted for any conduct during the pardon period, he has no legal exposure so long as he speaks truthfully.

For Fauci, that is a question that could be highly subjective. He referred to the risk of a "perjury trap" in his opening statement. He declared, "The only conclusion I can reach is that the sole reason he is calling me before this committee is to get me to say something — anything — that could vindicate his repeated public pledges that I end up, in his words, quote, ‘behind bars.’"

Even that statement could present a matter for litigation. Congress previously found in 2013 when high-ranking IRS leader Lois Lerner also pleaded the Fifth after giving an opening statement before the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. The Justice Department under the Obama administration refused to prosecute. Fauci will argue that such a general statement does not waive the privilege and that, when asked a question, he promptly and consistently invoked it.

Of course, this is the Trump administration, not the Obama Administration. Ironically, if the matter is litigated, the administration will be in the position of defending the pardon, which it has long questioned, as the result of Joe Biden's infamous autopen. The ability to hold Fauci in contempt becomes dependent on that pardon being valid.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: WHY FAUCI'S 111 FIFTH AMENDMENT PLEAS COULD END UP BEFORE THE COURTS

The Justice Department can argue that the Supreme Court has consistently held that the mere fear of a perjury charge is insufficient to compel witnesses who are immunized, dating back to 1896 in Brown v. Walker.

Moreover, the Supreme Court has held that "anticipatory perjury" is not a basis for such a refusal to testify in cases such as United States v. Apfelbaum.

However, Fauci can cite new state investigations as unaffected by the federal pardon, as well as new questions arising outside the pardon that could theoretically pose ongoing risks of criminal prosecution.

Courts have generally adopted broad interpretations to protect the right to remain silent, a touchstone of our legal system. That is why I believe Fauci likely has the edge in any challenge.

The fact is that it is uncertain. The cases in this area remain relatively sparse, and any pardon case is highly case-specific to the confines and scope of the specific pardon.

If so, Fauci can remain silent, but that silence will remain deafening for many in this country.

The right to do something does not make it the right thing to do. Fauci, in my view, was wrong to invoke the privilege against self-incrimination even if it was his right to do so. Millions of Americans lost loved ones during the pandemic, and the United States had one of the worst records in dealing with COVID-19 in terms of costs and deaths. Fauci's diaries exposed disturbing contradictions between what he previously stated publicly and what he actually believed. Americans have a right to know the truth, and Fauci was not saying a thing, invoking the privilege 111 times.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

He will say nothing to the families who lost loved ones or the business owners ruined by now-debunked pandemic measures.

ANTHONY FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY AND EMAILS SHOW HE KNEW LOCKDOWNS FAILED AND PUSHED MASKS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

He will say nothing to the scientists who were canceled, blacklisted, and fired for opposing these policies. Those scientists did not get the bobbleheads and celebrity photos that Fauci celebrated in his diaries. As the mob hounded them, Fauci said nothing as he gushed about his own fame in his diary.

He will say nothing despite the protection of a presidential pardon. For that, he should be rightfully condemned. Fauci's contempt of Congress is challengeable, but his contempt for the public is undeniable.

item.title: Panthers rally past Cardinals in Hall of Fame Game to open NFL preseason
item.description: Haynes King's rushing touchdown on the final play capped a stellar debut, but Carson Beck's sharp passing kept the Cardinals competitive throughout.
item.content:encoded:
Rookie quarterback Haynes King opened the NFL preseason with a last-play finish, scoring from 5 yards out to give the Carolina Panthers a 33-30 win over the Arizona Cardinals in the annual Hall of Fame Game.

The former Georgia Tech standout ended the night with 180 yards in the air and two touchdowns. He racked up 39 yards on the ground.

On the other sideline, fellow rookie Carson Beck gave Arizona an encouraging first look before his exhibition debut wrapped up.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Quarterback Kedon Slovis later put the Cardinals back ahead, throwing a 1-yard touchdown pass to Bryson Green with just under two minutes remaining for a 30-27 lead.

BEST BET FOR THE CAROLINA PANTHERS VS ARIZONA CARDINALS 2026 NFL PRO FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME GAME.

But King rallied the Panthers on a night when both teams elected to keep their starters on the sideline. Bryce Young was King's biggest cheerleader throughout the game.

King's 4-yard touchdown pass to Anthony Tyus III in the opening minute of the fourth quarter put Carolina ahead 24-20. He also threw a touchdown pass to Ja'Seem Reed in the second quarter.

Beck, a third-round pick from Miami, ended the night with 188 passing yards and one touchdown.

Quarterback Drew Brees, running back Roger Craig, kicker Adam Vinatieri, wide receiver Larry Fitzgerald and linebacker Luke Kuechly make up the Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2026.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump praises Team USA Winter Olympians and Paralympians at White House after record medal haul
item.description: Trump hosted over 120 Team USA Winter Olympians and Paralympians at the White House, celebrating a historic medal haul from the Milano Cortina Games.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump looked over his left and right shoulder, as well as in the crowd, as he hosted more than 120 Team USA Winter Olympians and Paralympians at the White House to celebrate their accomplishment at the Milano Cortina Games earlier this year.

There were 57 total medals brought back to the United States by the 300 athletes representing the Stars and Stripes, including 12 gold medals.

As Trump emphasized, it was a historic Winter Games for the Olympians, securing the most-ever U.S. gold medals in a single year. It was also the most medals won (33) by Team USA in a Winter Olympics outside North America.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

And 24 more medals came back to the States after 72 Paralympians competed across all five sports, securing 13 gold medals including a fifth straight sled hockey victory.

"Paralympians bring home their fifth straight gold medal in sled hockey, extending one of the greatest dynasties in all of international sports and it’s amazing what you’ve done. Nobody’s ever done anything like it," Trump said before acknowledging members from that team.

TRUMP URGES CONGRESS TO PASS PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT BEFORE RECESS: 'WE HAVE TO GET THAT DONE'

Speaking of hockey, Trump would be remiss not to mention the men’s and women’s Olympic hockey squads that both defeated Canada in overtime.

"The 2026 men’s Olympic hockey team. We celebrated together and it was really an incredible time. The women’s team and the men’s team — it was just incredible," Trump said.

"We can’t forget and never would — and nobody would have the courage to forget either because they are amazing. The history-making women’s hockey team. This team left everything on the ice."

Trump had previously invited members of the men’s Olympic hockey team to his State of the Union address just days after winning gold, where goaltender Connor Hellebuyck was given the Presidential Medal of Freedom earlier that day.

Trump received backlash for making a joking remark during a call with the men’s team following their overtime victory that he would be "impeached" if he didn’t invite the women to the White House for an event as well. USA Hockey released a statement later that, while athletes were grateful for the invitation, their active college and pro schedules made attendance impossible.

But forwards Joy Dunne and Abbey Murphy were both among the Olympians and Paralympians behind Trump on Thursday at the White House. He took time during his speech to recognize both of them.

After congratulating every member of Team USA in his speech, Trump was gifted a Team USA varsity jacket and a new pair of shoes as mementos for what was an incredible performance all around by those representing the country.

Those who were unable to attend the event on Thursday were already back training for the 2030 Olympic and Paralympic Games , which will be held in the French Alps .

In 2034, Salt Lake City will be the host site for the Winter Games, which Trump was excited to mention.

item.title: Aces star targets heckling Fever fans in Indy before Chelsea Gray stuns Caitlin Clark in OT thriller
item.description: Jackie Young called for security to remove two courtside fans as the Las Vegas Aces edged the Indiana Fever 86-84 in a dramatic overtime thriller.
item.content:encoded:
This is the most the WNBA has done to keep men out of its sport.

During Thursday night's WILD battle between the Indiana Fever and Las Vegas Aces at Gainbridge Fieldhouse, venue security confronted several men seated courtside who were making noise.

Las Vegas' Jackie Young took time out of a tight game to confront the fans and actively demanded that security handle them. The Amazon Prime Video commentators even celebrated as the men were shown being escorted off the floor. Young finished with 22 points, but her biggest effort was causing a floor-side scene over paying customers.

SOME WNBA PLAYERS ACT LIKE THEY ARE THE ONLY ONES WHO RECEIVE MEAN SOCIAL MEDIA MESSAGES

Welcome to the modern WNBA, where ordinary courtside heckling can apparently become a five-alarm emergency. The optics are ridiculous for a league demanding more eyeballs. When authentic, rowdy sports-fan culture shows up, suddenly everyone acts like they need a safe space.

But the fan drama was only the beginning of the chaos on the hardwood.

The Aces, holding the second-best record in the WNBA, found themselves in an absolute dogfight with Indiana. A'ja Wilson paced Las Vegas with 26 points in a crazy contest featuring nine lead changes between the fourth quarter and overtime alone.

Indiana had victory in its grasp down the stretch, but Caitlin Clark had a sloppy night, finishing with 20 points, eight assists, and three rebounds alongside a whopping eight turnovers. Clark's worst regulation blunder came at the charity stripe, where she uncharacteristically missed two crucial free throws that surrendered Indiana's lead and left the door wide open for Las Vegas.

CAITLIN CLARK ERUPTS FOR 32 POINTS AS FEVER HOLD OFF STORM TO COMPLETE SEASON-SERIES SWEEP

Aces veteran Chelsea Gray made Indiana pay, draining a clutch buzzer-beater to tie the game at 75-75 and force overtime.

Then Clark choked again.

With Indiana clinging to an 84-83 lead in overtime, Clark coughed up a crushing turnover that gave Las Vegas final possession. Gray capitalized once more, knocking down a cold-blooded three-pointer as time expired to secure an 86-84 victory for the Aces.

After the game, an Indiana Fever spokesperson told OutKick-Fox News that security found no violation of the Fan Code of Conduct and that the fan was not ejected, but instead "elected to leave."

FORMER FEVER PLAYER RESPONDS TO SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM BY ALLEGING INDIANA HARASSMENT COVER-UP

In the end, running to venue security because front-row banter hurt your feelings sends a terrible message to the paying fans funding your chartered flights.

The WNBA wants the crowds, the attention and the money that come with big-time professional sports. Fine. But that means taking the heckling, too.

Stop playing arena fun police and let fans be fans.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

item.title: Trump-backed incumbent loses primary after super PAC bankrolled by Dems meddled in race
item.description: A super PAC bankrolled by a California billionaire and frequent Democratic donor spent $2 million to unseat Andy Ogles over renewable energy policy.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., was defeated in a primary challenge on Thursday evening by Republican challenger Charlie Hatcher, a farmer and the state's former commissioner of agriculture.

Although the primary was far from a top-watched contest coming into the 2026 primaries, it served as a microcosm of larger forces at play in the Republican Party. From a break in endorsements between President Donald Trump and Tennessee’s Republican Governor Bill Lee to millions being pumped into the district over environmental policy, the race attracted attention well beyond its borders.

The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition super PAC had spent roughly $2 million opposing Ogles and supporting Hatcher. The group has raised $6.7 million this year, making Ogles a sizable portion of their spending this cycle.

TOP TRUMP ALLY WARNS SUPER PAC BANKROLLED BY DEM BILLIONAIRE IS MEDDLING IN GOP PRIMARY

The way that Ogles sees it, it’s an attempt to show Republicans what happens when lawmakers attempt to claw back government funding for renewable energy sources.

Like many other Republicans, Ogles has called to scale back renewable energy investments made under the Biden Administration.

"When you have a group spending roughly $2 million in a Republican primary, that tells you how much money they're making off of government subsidies, and they're upset that the government welfare has been taken away from them," Ogles told Fox News Digital in an interview.

A Fox News Digital review of FEC filings discovered that the super PAC is bankrolled by Chris Larsen, the California-based billionaire chairman of Ripple, a financial technology company that, according to its website, offers crypto solutions for businesses.

Larsen is also a frequent Democratic donor, having contributed $5,444,975 to support Kamala Harris's failed presidential campaign.

More than just his opposition to government-backed renewable energy initiatives, Ogles thinks it’s his proximity to Trump that has made him a target.

"It's because I'm close to the president. It is because I am outspoken. And quite frankly, it is because I speak plainly on these issues," Ogles said.

GOP GOVERNOR ENDORSES CANDIDATE CHALLENGING TRUMP-BACKED CONGRESSMAN IN REPUBLICAN US HOUSE PRIMARY

For his own part, Hatcher, a fifth-generation Tennessee dairy farmer, has pitched himself as someone unencumbered by the political scene and ensnaring interests.

"I think there’s something missing in Washington. There’s a lack of farmer common sense. There’s a lack of work ethic. One of my strengths is problem-solving, looking for solutions, looking for collaborations and supporting the Trump Administration and Speaker Johnson on their agenda," Hatcher said in a campaign video.

Notably, Tennessee’s Republican governor put his weight behind Hatcher late on Tuesday evening, citing a personal relationship between them.

"He served as my commissioner of agriculture; I know Charlie. I know his conservative values and how much he loves our country. Charlie has stood with President Trump since day one," Lee said in a video.

Trump, who has endorsed Ogles, reaffirmed his support for the conservative firebrand ahead of the primary.

"Andy will be really enshrined as one of the best congressmen that you’ll ever see. He’s just fantastic," Trump said. "Andy has always been there when we needed him and when I needed him. He’s been a great help. He’s been a source of inspiration to a lot of people in Congress," Trump said in a post to Truth Social earlier this year.

TENNESSEE PASSES NEW CONGRESSIONAL MAP LIKELY TO FLIP FINAL DEM SEAT AS PROTESTS ERUPT INSIDE CAPITOL

Having captured the Republican nomination, Hatcher now advances to a general election he’s heavily favored to win on Nov. 3. He won re-election in 2024 in a 56.9% to 39.5% victory over Maryam Abolfazli.

item.title: Mamdani repeatedly sidesteps questions on reported plan to revive tax hikes on wealthy New Yorkers
item.description: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani repeatedly declined to address reports of a fall campaign to build support for higher taxes on wealthy residents and corporations.
item.content:encoded:
New York City democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani repeatedly sidestepped questions Thursday about reported plans to launch a public pressure campaign this fall pushing tax hikes on wealthy New Yorkers and corporations.

Mamdani reportedly plans to build public support after Labor Day for similar proposals that Gov. Kathy Hochul previously rejected in early 2026. The reported push is expected ahead of the New York Legislature's return to Albany in January 2027 and Hochul's re-election campaign this fall, according to The New York Post.

During an interview with Fox 5 New York, Mamdani repeatedly declined to answer questions about the potential campaign before later saying such discussions would only come after the November election.

Asked whether he had spoken with Hochul about the reported campaign, Mamdani did not answer directly, instead using the opportunity to tout the opening of 2,000 free child care seats for New Yorkers through their policy efforts.

NYC MAYOR MAMDANI CALLS THREAT OF RICH PEOPLE LEAVING NYC OVER TAXES 'IMAGINED'

"The governor and I are in constant communication and, frankly, I appreciate her partnership because if it wasn't for the governor, then we wouldn't have been able to stand together to announce that we had more than 5,000 New Yorkers come forward to apply for these 2,000 free child care seats," he said. "And I'm so excited about that, and the fact that we're going to expand to 12,000, and the work that's still to come."

The reporter then pressed Mamdani on whether the Democratic Socialists of America would join the potential campaign this fall, but he again declined to answer directly, saying his focus remains on the present.

BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS

"My focus right now is where we are, which is August, and ensuring that everything that we're doing is keeping New Yorkers safe amidst a heat wave and preparing for the school year," Mamdani said. "A lot of the conversation about what comes after November, I think, is a conversation for what comes after November."

"So you don't plan to launch a campaign to tax the rich before the November election?" the reporter asked.

"The conversations I've been having with the governor and with my team are about the here and now and there will always be time for the conversations that come after that," Mamdani said.

MAMDANI EXTENDS DEADLINE FOR NYC HOMEOWNERS TO SEEK EXEMPTION FROM NEW PIED-À-TERRE TAX

The reported campaign would revive a previous push by Mamdani to close the city's multibillion-dollar budget gap through tax increases, a proposal Hochul previously rejected. Mamdani's earlier plan called for raising the city's personal income tax rate on filers earning $1 million or more, a move he projected could generate roughly $3 billion annually, while also increasing corporate tax rates.

As an alternative, Hochul and Mamdani jointly advanced the state's first pied-à-terre tax, an annual surcharge on certain high-value second homes, which passed in May 2026. State and city officials have projected the measure could raise about $500 million annually.

Mamdani also said his May 2026 executive budget closed what his administration described as an inherited $12 billion budget gap, crediting aggressive savings, new investments, his partnership with Albany and new tax revenue, including the pied-à-terre tax.

Mamdani's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

item.title: Trump urges Congress to pass Protect College Sports Act before recess: 'We have to get that done'
item.description: Trump urged Congress to pass the Protect College Sports Act at a White House event honoring Team USA Winter Olympic athletes, saying he would sign it immediately.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump has once again urged lawmakers to pass the Protect College Sports Act, saying "we have to get that done" as Congress recess looms.

Trump had more than 120 athletes, coaches, staff and representatives from Team USA for a special celebration at the White House on Thursday night to celebrate their achievements at the Milano Cortina Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games.

As Trump referenced "the collegiate athletic system is the engine of American Olympic dominance," producing 88% of the Team USA representatives in those Games alone, he urged the House and Senate to pass the bill, which he said he would sign immediately at his desk.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"I’m urging the House and the Senate to come together, bipartisan if possible and it looks like they have done, to send the bill to my desk and I will sign it. I think we have no choice," Trump said. "We have to get that done. If we don’t, we’re very foolish. Nobody knows what will happen. We’re in Never-Never Land. We’re not going to let that be happening. We’re not going to let that happen to these great people and others."

Trump added that his administration is "doing everything we can to protect the cherished sporting traditions that have long been a part of our nation."

DONALD TRUMP SAYS COLLEGE SPORTS 'TURNING INTO PRO SPORTS' WITH NO RULES, URGES FOR BIPARTISAN BILL TO SIGN

"Already we’ve done a lot to save women’s sports, and we’re also saving college sports. We’re in the process of working very hard," he said.

The Protect College Sports Act, a bipartisan bill that NCAA officials continue to lobby lawmakers to pass, would provide the collegiate governing body with greater antitrust legal protections while also establishing a uniform framework for college athletics in terms of Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) compensation, the transfer portal and more.

The bill, though, has had its obstacles in the Senate, including Thursday when three Republican senators filed an amendment aimed at preventing the bill from overriding state laws that bar biological men from competing in women’s sports. Sens. Josh Hawley of Missouri, Jim Banks of Indiana and Tommy Tuberville of Alabama are pushing to close what they view as a loophole to undo laws in their states designed to keep biological males out of women’s sports.

The bill’s current writing would override certain state laws dealing with college athlete eligibility, and these senators believe their laws, as well as similar ones in other states, would be impacted, leading to their amendment to make clear those state laws remain in effect if the bill passed.

"I’ve reviewed the current draft of the Senate NIL bill and I am very concerned it PREEMPTS Missouri’s law banning men in women’s sports," Hawley wrote on X. "This is what [Riley Gaines] has been saying. Big, big problem."

REPUBLICAN SENATORS FILE AMENDMENT TO STOP COLLEGE SPORTS BILL FROM OVERRIDING STATE WOMEN'S SPORTS LAWS

While word of the amendment has yet to come, and could play a significant role in Republican support, Trump hopes the bill itself heads to the Oval Office sooner than later with the framework needed to protect college sports now and in the future. Earlier on Thursday, the Trump administration issued a statement supporting the passage of the act, reaffirming the president’s wish to see a college sports bill passed.

"The future of college sports, especially the future of Olympic and non-revenue sports, is threatened by significant legal and financial uncertainty. Federal legislative action is imperative to fix the statutory ambiguities, ensure liability protection and uniform standards, and stop the endless litigation that is fueling this crisis, which will in turn provide the stability, fairness, and balance necessary to protect student-athletes and preserve collegiate athletic opportunities," the statement of administration policy read.

But there is the Congress recess to think about. The Senate is set for its five-week recess when the day concludes on Friday, though it faces a big to-do list other than just attempting to pass this bill which could delay leaving Capitol Hill.

Whether the Senate checks the Protect College Sports Act off that list remains to be seen, but Trump gave a Thursday night nudge in hopes it reaches the House, and soon after, his desk.

item.title: Retired police chief helps subdue passenger after alleged midair outburst over alcohol cutoff
item.description: Retired Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O'Hara described the 45-minute ordeal aboard a United Airlines flight before he and two off-duty deputies acted.
item.content:encoded:
Retired Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O'Hara found himself back in crisis mode Thursday, not on the streets of Mill City, but 35,000 feet in the air, when what should have been a routine United Airlines flight suddenly turned chaotic.

O'Hara told Fox News Digital he watched flight attendants spend nearly 45 minutes trying to de-escalate an increasingly belligerent passenger, prompting him and two off-duty Bergen County, New Jersey, sheriff's deputies to intervene.

The retired police chief, who was traveling with his wife aboard United Flight 1364 from Newark to Fort Lauderdale, said the passenger repeatedly berated flight attendants, tried to get out of his seat and behaved erratically as crew members worked to keep the situation under control.

FRONTIER PASSENGERS TACKLE MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY CHOKED OFF-DUTY FLIGHT ATTENDANT, TRIED TO OPEN DOOR MID-FLIGHT

"About like for the last 45 minutes of the flight ... all the flight attendants came over, and they were incredible," O'Hara told Fox News Digital. "Incredibly professional, just trying to talk to this guy to de-escalate things."

According to O'Hara, the passenger became increasingly agitated after flight attendants refused to serve him more alcohol, a detail O'Hara said he later learned from the Broward Sheriff's Office after the arrest. The man reportedly continued shouting profanities and making threatening remarks before the encounter turned physical.

"It was infuriating to hear a man speak to these women who were just incredibly professional and trying to keep everybody safe that way for so long," O'Hara said. "And, finally, he just kind of got up and lunged towards them."

That's when two passengers seated near the back of the aircraft grabbed the man from behind as O'Hara rushed forward from his seat.

OFF-DUTY TROOPER AND ARMED CITIZEN HAILED AS HEROES AFTER RETURNING FIRE ON IN-N-OUT GUNMAN

The three men worked together to restrain the passenger using plastic flex cuffs before securing him back in his seat, so the flight attendants could take their seats and the plane could land safely.

O'Hara later learned the two passengers were Bergen County Sheriff's deputies from New Jersey.

United Airlines also confirmed the incident in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Local law enforcement met United Flight 1364 upon its arrival in Fort Lauderdale to address an unruly passenger," the airline said. "We thank our crew and customers for assisting with the situation and helping ensure the safety of everyone onboard."

UNITED FLIGHT FROM CHICAGO MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER PASSENGER'S 'MULTIPLE ATTEMPTS' TO BREACH COCKPIT

The airline said the Boeing 737-900 was carrying 174 passengers and six crew members, including two pilots and four flight attendants.

While cellphone video of the confrontation has circulated widely on social media, O'Hara said it doesn't capture the nearly hour-long effort by the flight crew to peacefully resolve the situation before passengers stepped in.

"No one should take the kind of verbal abuse that they did," he said. "They were absolute professionals trying to keep everybody safe."

O'Hara, who spent 25 years in law enforcement before retiring after leading public safety operations in Newark, New Jersey, and later serving as Minneapolis police chief, said the incident underscored just how dangerous violent outbursts can become aboard an aircraft.

"I started to think, ‘Well, geez, what are we going to do if somebody really wants to fight the whole time?’" he said. "It's dangerous. We're in such a confined space like that, and someone's going to act out like that because you don't know potentially what the motivation might be."

His wife, who is a lieutenant with the Newark Police Department, was seated nearby throughout the ordeal.

"The only thing I was thinking about was if this goes bad, I know at least she has my back," O'Hara said with a laugh, adding he has seen her "handle herself on the street" and knew she would be ready if the situation worsened.

Afterward, O'Hara's wife praised her husband's actions in a social media post.

"Proud of my husband today," she wrote. "When a disruptive passenger created a dangerous situation on a flight, he stepped up to help federal agents safely arrest him. Leadership isn’t just about the job you hold, it’s about being willing to help when others need it. Grateful everyone on board arrived safely."

Looking back on the incident, O'Hara said he hopes Americans choose action over standing by when innocent people are in danger.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

"We're coming up on the 25th anniversary of September 11," he said. "I would hope everybody in this country now knows that if things are escalating to the point where there's going to be some kind of violence, I think every citizen that is able to has a duty to try and help to stop it."

He also said airlines should ensure restraints are readily available and that crew members are trained to use them if passengers become violent.

"I think it would be good to make sure that they have restraints that are available, that at least some people are trained in some way to use them safely to get somebody restrained if they needed to," O'Hara said.

As of Thursday afternoon, authorities had not publicly identified the passenger or announced any criminal charges.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Broward Sheriff's Office and the Federal Aviation Administration for additional information and comment.

item.title: Squad-backed ‘Tennessee Three’ lawmaker wins House primary in newly redrawn district
item.description: Squad-backed 'Tennessee Three' lawmaker Justin Pearson won the Democrat primary in Tennessee's redrawn 9th Congressional District after redistricting split the Memphis-area district.
item.content:encoded:
Squad-backed Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson, District 86, part of the trio of lawmakers in his state referred to as the "Tennessee Three," won the Democratic primary Thursday in Tennessee's newly redrawn 9th Congressional District.

Pearson defeated state Sen. London Lamar, District 33, community activist Marion LaTroy Alexandria-Williams and attorney Jim Torino. He will face Brent Taylor, the Republican nominee who was endorsed by President Donald Trump, in November with his campaign warchest of millions of dollars he has raised throughout his campaign, significantly outpacing his Democratic opponents.

The Memphis-area state lawmaker entered the primary with the backing of prominent Democrats who are part of the progressive group of lawmakers called "the Squad," including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., and Summer Lee, D-Pa., who all joined Pearson at a campaign rally in Memphis last month.

'SQUAD' MEMBER'S COMEBACK BID THWARTED AS ESTABLISHMENT DEMS NOTCH VICTORY AGAINST SOCIALISTS

Known for his fiery, preacher-style speeches, Pearson has also received support from national left-wing groups including Justice Democrats, the Working Families Party, MoveOn and Indivisible.

Pearson rose to national prominence in 2023 as one of the "Tennessee Three" lawmakers who participated in a gun-control protest on the state House floor following the Covenant School shooting in Nashville that killed three young kids and three adults.

Republican lawmakers subsequently expelled Pearson and fellow state Rep. Justin Jones over the protest, though they later regained their seats. 

A third Democrat, Gloria Johnson of Knoxville, avoided expulsion by a single vote, according to local media reporting.

'JUMPING SHIP': HOUSE DEM FINDS EXIT STRATEGY AFTER SCOTUS RULING SHIFTS ADVANTAGE TO GOP

The open-seat primary won by Pearson on Thursday followed a redrawing of Tennessee’s congressional map that divided Memphis among three Republican-leaning districts and prompted longtime Democratic Rep. Steve Cohen, D-Tenn., to retire.

Before the new map, heavily Democratic Memphis was largely kept together in the 9th District, giving Tennessee Democrats one reliable congressional seat in an otherwise deeply Republican state.

Cohen has been the lone Democrat in Tennessee’s nine-member House delegation alongside eight Republicans since 2023, but the new map favors the GOP in all nine districts.

item.title: Conservative firebrand who went viral with anti-CCP ad survives key primary
item.description: Marsha Blackburn defeated John Rose and Monty Fritts in the Tennessee GOP primary, positioning her as the likely next governor of the state.
item.content:encoded:
U.S. Senator Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., cruised to victory in a GOP primary on Thursday evening in a race to replace outgoing Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee.

With the nomination in tow, Blackburn is likely to become the next governor in the Volunteer State — a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to its top executive role since 2006. 

Lee, who has served in the role since 2019, is term-limited and cannot seek re-election. He last won reelection in a 64.9% to 32.9% victory over Democratic challenger Jason Martin, a businessman and doctor.

DEMS RALLY AROUND BEST HOPE TO DEFEND GOVERNOR'S MANSION FROM GOP TAKEOVER

Notably, Lee did not endorse anyone in the three-way Republican race for the 2026 nomination but noted that he had a close relationship with Blackburn when she announced her candidacy.

"I’ve been friends with Marsha for a long time, and she served as my congressman and representative in the General Assembly. I’m proud we have really good people running for governor in this state," Lee told local outlets.

Blackburn, for her own part, promised to continue focusing on issues that Republicans have made centerpieces to the GOP platform in Washington, D.C.

She highlighted immigration as one such issue.

"As governor, I’ll deport illegals, stop the flow of drugs and drug money. We will crack down on Cartels, restrict cash transfers to drug havens and hit criminals and illegals where it hurts — in their wallets," Blackburn said in a campaign video.

Blackburn also promised to prevent China from buying up Tennessee land, punctuating her commitment with a viral ad where she crushed a fortune cookie.

"It doesn’t take a fortune cookie to figure it out. Here in Tennessee we’re going to stop communist China and protect Tennessee land," she remarked.

President Donald Trump also did not issue an endorsement in the race, saying that he had ties to one of Blackburn’s challengers: Rep. John Rose, R-Tenn.

TRUMP MAY HAVE ENDORSED DARLINE GRAHAM, BUT GOP SENATE HOPEFULS AREN’T BACKING DOWN

Rose, an 8th-generation farmer and the millionaire founder of Transcender Corp., an IT certification company, has served in the Tennessee legislature since 2019. In his gubernatorial campaign, he pitched himself as a homegrown candidate focused on local solutions to local problems.

"I know that anything is achievable in Tennessee because I have lived it. Now, I’m asking for you to give me the chance to bring opportunity to all Tennesseans," Rose said in a campaign video.

On his website, Rose highlighted five key areas of focus, including education, infrastructure, healthcare, energy and economic and community development.

A third candidate, State Rep. Monty Fritts, had run on a more aggressive, small-government platform.

"My number one priority is leaving more money in your pockets, in your purses and in your country bankrolls rather than sending it to Nashville," Fritts said in a campaign video.

On his website, Fritts touted positions like shrinking the size of Tennessee’s budget, protecting citizen rights against encroaching government power and increasing parent input in education.

Fritts attracted controversy earlier this year when, as part of his campaign, he called for a ban on mosques and other "pagan religions."

5 MEXICAN CARTEL BOSSES CHARGED IN WEAPONS, DRUG TRAFFICKING, TIMESHARE FRAUD SCHEMES, DOJ SAYS

"Islam is a little different story than perhaps other religions are, in that it’s not necessarily a religion; it’s a political movement," Fritts said. "It’s that movement that, if you don’t submit, perhaps you are executed. I feel that Islam is incongruent with both our U.S. and Tennessee Constitution," Fritts told local outlets.

Having cleared the primary, Blackburn will run in the state’s general election on Nov. 3 against her Democratic opponent, Memphis City Councilwoman and Chief Public Defender Jerri Green.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Oversight Project sues to block Maryland Democrats’ redistricting measure backed by Gov Moore
item.description: A redistricting lawsuit alleges Maryland officials missed mandatory deadlines for HB 2100 and used a last-minute clause to bypass certification rules.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: A new lawsuit set to be filed in Maryland seeks to block a redistricting amendment backed by Democrat Gov. Wes Moore from appearing on the November ballot, arguing state officials advanced the measure after the state's own legislative analysts concluded the statutory deadline for certifying ballot questions had already passed.

The complaint, filed Thursday night in Anne Arundel County Circuit Court by the conservative watchdog group Oversight Project and reviewed by Fox News Digital, argues HB 2100 could not lawfully reach voters because Maryland's July 1 deadline for certifying statewide ballot questions expired more than a month before lawmakers convened a special session to approve the proposal.

The Oversight Project, which filed the lawsuit with Republican lawmakers, argues approval of the amendment could pave the way for an 8-0 Democratic congressional delegation. 

SUPREME COURT DEALS BLOW TO VIRGINIA DEMOCRATS IN FIGHT OVER STATE COURT ELECTION MAP RULING

HB 2100 would ask voters to amend the Maryland Constitution so state constitutional standards governing compactness and boundaries would no longer apply to congressional districts.

The Oversight Project describes itself as working "to expose and root out corruption in government, among elected officials, and in our most influential organizations to ensure power resides with the American People."

Its filing points to a Department of Legislative Services fiscal note stating that "the new statutory deadline of July 1 for certification of ballot questions" had already passed. The fiscal note also states that election officials were required to publicly post the full text of a proposed constitutional amendment at least 90 days before Election Day.

According to the complaint, lawmakers then added the phrase "notwithstanding any other provision of law" to HB 2100 less than an hour before the joint committee hearing began. The plaintiffs argue the language was intended to override Maryland's certification, notice and public comment requirements after those deadlines had already elapsed.

The complaint further alleges Democratic sponsors characterized the amendment as merely "technical" in the House, while Senate debate reflected that lawmakers understood the statutory timeline could no longer be met.

The filing cites remarks by Democratic state Sen. Cheryl Kagan during floor debate.

VIRGINIA DEMS ACCUSED OF ILLEGALLY ‘STEAMROLLING’ STATE LAW THAT COULD UPEND REDISTRICTING CRUSADE

"There is no time to comply with the plain language of the law with our new law because July 1st is in the rearview mirror," Kagan said, according to the complaint. "There's no time to have the Secretary of State draft language, to have it published, to have a comment period, to have it modified. It's just not an option."

Maryland GOP Delegate Matt Morgan, one of the plaintiffs, told Fox News Digital the disputed language was introduced at 11:08 a.m. for a noon committee hearing.

"They have the law. They're supposed to follow it. They didn't," Morgan said. "And now we're going to take it to court and see what the judges have to say about it."

DEMS CIRCLE THE WAGONS BY BLAMING GOP FOR THEIR GERRYMANDERING RESPONSE AHEAD OF MIDTERMS: 'VERY DESPERATE'

Morgan said Democratic leadership later described the amendment as "technical" on the House floor.

"The truth is that that was their way of trying to get around them missing all these statutory deadlines," he said.

Republican Delegate Kathy Szeliga, another plaintiff, said legislators had only hours to review the revised language while the public had no opportunity to comment.

"The public got absolutely no time to look and weigh in on the amended language," Szeliga told Fox News Digital. "So, it just reeks of a naked political, partisan power grab on the Democrats' behalf."

According to the complaint, the proposal is intended to overturn the practical effect of a 2022 state court ruling holding that those constitutional standards applied to congressional redistricting. Democrats hold seven of Maryland's eight U.S. House seats.

REDISTRICTING WAR INTENSIFIES AS GOP SUFFERS SETBACKS IN TWO STATES

Moore has publicly defended the amendment as a response to Republican-led redistricting efforts in other states, saying it would ensure "Marylanders — and no one else — have the final say over their representation."

The lawsuit asks the court to bar state officials from certifying, printing, distributing, tabulating or canvassing votes on the amendment and requests expedited review because of the approaching election calendar.

Moore's office, the Maryland Attorney General's Office and the Maryland State Board of Elections did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

item.title: NYC church arson suspect allegedly plotted more attacks, had violent notes like 'murder them' and 'rape him'
item.description: A homeless man admitted to setting fire to the 173-year-old South Bushwick Reformed Church, and prosecutors revealed a notebook with violent target lists.
item.content:encoded:
A homeless man accused of an arson attack on a historic New York City church admitted to burning the religious site, and prosecutors said he kept disturbing lists of targets of violence with categories such as "kill them" and "rape him" as he mapped out more fire attacks.

John Jones, 24, was arrested Wednesday and admitted to law enforcement he set fire to the South Bushwick Reformed Church, sparking a three-alarm fire that torched the 173-year-old church June 19, according to a detention memo filed by federal prosecutors, the New York Post reported.

"The defendant admitted to committing the church arson for which he has been charged in this case," the memo states. "Furthermore, the defendant stated that he had recently attempted to burn down a second church in Brooklyn, New York."

Prosecutors also said in the memo that they discovered Jones' notebook that included a chart with several handwritten categories for violent targets, including "murder them," "kill them," "stab them," "make them pay" and "rape him."

HISTORIC NYC CHURCH ENGULFED IN 5-ALARM BLAZE; 6 FIREFIGHTERS INJURED BATTLING STUBBORN FLAMES

The categories, which are featured as part of a chart, include tally marks and repeated misspellings of the word "church," prosecutors said.

Jones was charged with arson in the South Bushwick Reformed Church fire. He faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted.

Prosecutors said they wish to hold Jones without bail. He is expected to be arraigned Friday.

"This defendant placed countless Brooklyn residents at risk when he recklessly set fire to the South Bushwick Reformed Church in broad daylight," NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement. 

"New Yorkers deserve to practice their faith freely and without fear, and the destruction of this sacred New York City landmark will be met with swift justice."

Jones was linked to the fire after he was captured on surveillance video attempting to enter the church, according to the criminal complaint.

He was denied entry and then walked across the street to buy a lighter. He then appeared in video footage returning to the side of the church, and surveillance footage showed a large plume of smoke rising from the building shortly afterward, prosecutors said.

The three-alarm fire gutted much of the historic church and destroyed its historic spire, causing it to collapse. Thousands of historic artifacts were also lost to the fire, which torched the inside of the building.

WOMAN ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY BEHEADING JESUS STATUE OUTSIDE CATHOLIC CHURCH

The church was constructed in the 1850s and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1982. It was also designated as a New York City landmark in 1968.

"The intentional burning of a house of worship is an attack on a historic building and on the sense of safety and community it represents," FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said in a statement. 

"This fire placed lives at risk, including the first responders who responded to protect the church and the surrounding neighborhood."

Jones was taken into custody Wednesday after he was caught at a Midtown Manhattan CVS attempting to shoplift, according to the New York Post. He made an appearance Thursday in Manhattan Criminal Court to be arraigned on the shoplifting charge, and he was held without bail.

item.title: Old Trails Fire suspect allegedly confessed to setting 25 fires; judge doubles bail to $2M
item.description: Aaron Forrest Farinacci allegedly confessed to setting 25 fires and modeling a delayed ignition device after serial arsonist John Leonard Orr.
item.content:encoded:
The man accused of starting the devastating Old Trails Fire in Spokane County had his bail doubled to $2 million Thursday after prosecutors filed four additional arson charges and alleged he admitted to setting 25 fires in the area since 2025.

Court documents reviewed by Fox News Digital allege Aaron Forrest Farinacci, 37, also confessed to monitoring weather apps to identify ideal conditions and checking weather conditions while constructing a delayed ignition device to start the Old Trails Fire.

During a court appearance Thursday, Judge Jeremy Schmidt found probable cause to charge Farinacci with the four additional counts of first-degree arson stemming from fires allegedly set since last summer.

According to an arrest affidavit, Farinacci initially denied involvement in the Old Trails Fire during a 90-minute interrogation after his Aug. 3 arrest before later confessing to planning and setting the blaze alight.

WASHINGTON WILDFIRE ARSON SUSPECT PREVIOUSLY CHARGED WITH FIRST-DEGREE MURDER, RECORDS SHOW

Detectives also said they corroborated evidence linking Farinacci to other blazes — the Aubrey White, Copper River/Meenach, Fort George and Indian Bluff fires.

In court, Spokane County Prosecutor Preston McCollam asked for higher bond, stating, "I am asking the court to increase bail or bond in this amount to $2 million, given the gravity of these charges, given the addition of four separate arson counts."

SPOKANE FIRE SURVIVOR FINDS 'JOY' THROUGH JESUS AFTER ALLEGED ARSON DESTROYS HOME AND BELONGINGS

The judge agreed, noting, "The amount, as requested by prosecutor McCollam, is appropriate."

The arraignment was also delayed Thursday after Farinacci's defense requested a mental competency evaluation to determine whether he is fit to stand trial.

The expanded charges come amid widespread destruction caused by the Old Trails Fire, which started Aug. 1.

The blaze burned more than 3,200 acres, destroyed about 700 homes and other buildings and resulted the evacuation of more than 60,000 residents.

VIRGIN MARY STATUE BECOMES BEACON OF HOPE AFTER CALIFORNIA WILDFIRES, FOX NATION EXPLORES

Court documents also show Farinacci eventually admitted to planning the Old Trails Fire for two weeks.

The documents say he built a time-delay device from paper, matches, cigarettes and rubber bands modeled after one used by serial arsonist John Leonard Orr.

Documents also allege Farinacci deliberately ignited simultaneous fires at other times to distract and thin out emergency response crews.

Background checks also showed a prior conviction for manslaughter after he fatally shot his father in Arizona in 2010. He served about a decade in prison after pleading guilty in 2012 to manslaughter and aggravated assault. 

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: How Eric Bieniemy stays engaged with Chiefs while tending to wife, who recovers from alleged shooting by son
item.description: Eric Bieniemy is watching Chiefs practices via live feed and called Andy Reid in the middle of a drill while working remotely as his wife recovers from allegedly being shot by their son.
item.content:encoded:
Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy is dealing with a family tragedy after his son, Elijah, allegedly shot his wife, Mia, multiple times July 26, leaving her hospitalized.

But Chiefs GM Brett Veach said Bieniemy remains engaged with the team, though his family takes top priority.

Veach told reporters the team set up Bieniemy with a live feed of practices so he can watch and analyze remotely as players go through drills, according to The Athletic.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Veach said Bieniemy called him during one of the practices, asking to speak with head coach Andy Reid, who brought his old offensive coordinator back to the organization this offseason.

"That’s the thing. … It’s so refreshing to have back — that attention to detail," Veach said of Bieniemy, who wanted Reid to relay a message to rookie running back Emmett Johnson. "He demands each player knows his assignment. There’s never a safe space with him."

ERIC BIENIEMY'S SON JAILED FOR SHOOTING HIS MOTHER WHILE KANSAS CITY CHIEFS COACH IS AWAY AT TRAINING CAMP

Veach added that Bieniemy was brought back to give the roster a "kick in the a--," and he means that in the best way possible.

The Chiefs went 6-11 last season, a far cry from the success they’re used to. This is a group that was on the precipice of a dynasty, and depending on who you talk to, they might have even been one.

Bieniemy knows this team well, winning two Super Bowls with the franchise. The Chiefs are hoping his direction can bring them back to that level of football.

"Him being out there and hearing that voice, whether it be ‘Finish’ or ‘Alignment’ or whatever … he demands that you are buttoned up on your details, and that is a mirror image of coach and how he wants things run," Veach said, via The Athletic.

There’s no telling when Bieniemy will be heard again in person, though, after his 57-year-old wife was shot by their 27-year-old son at home in Ashburn, Va. Mia was critically wounded but has since been transferred out of an ICU.

Elijah was charged with malicious wounding, use of a firearm in the commission of a felony and discharge of a firearm inside a dwelling, per a press release by the Loudoun County Sheriff’s Office.

ERIC BIENIEMY’S SON BELIEVED TO HAVE CALLED COPS SAYING 'HIS PARENTS' CUT OFF HIS ACCESS TO WEAPONS: REPORT

A person believed to be Elijah reportedly called police two days before he allegedly shot his mother, saying he could not access his weapons from "his parents," according to the outlet. Elijah said his parents "are withholding his weapons and that he’s a certified UFC fighter, so now he feels like he cannot defend himself."

Elijah will not make a court appearance until he undergoes a mental health competency evaluation, court records showed. He "appears to suffer from significant mental health issues," and he "does not appear able to assist in his own defense at the present time."

Before returning to the Chiefs, Bieniemy spent time with the Washington Commanders, Chicago Bears and UCLA’s program.

The 56-year-old continues to attend to family matters, but he is helping the Chiefs as training camp really picks up this week.

item.title: Bodycam shows police K-9 leaping into action after suspected impaired driver refused to surrender
item.description: Body camera footage shows K-9 Midas leaping through a car window to end a 40-minute standoff with a suspected impaired driver in Vancouver, Washington.
item.content:encoded:
A suspected impaired driver who refused to surrender during a 40-minute standoff in Washington was finally taken into custody after police deployed a K-9 through the driver's side window, newly released body camera footage shows.

The Vancouver Police Department released body camera and dash camera footage Thursday from a July 26 incident involving a lengthy pursuit that ended with K-9 Midas leaping through the driver's side window to help officers arrest the suspect.

Police said they responded after receiving multiple reports of a driver who appeared to be impaired, had passed out behind the wheel and was allegedly inhaling from compressed air cans while driving.

VIDEO SHOWS ALLEGED CAR THIEF DANGLE UNDER BRIDGE AFTER WILD CHASE, SPARKING TENSE STANDOFF WITH POLICE

After officers located the vehicle and observed the driver continuing to inhale from a can, they attempted to conduct a traffic stop.

Police said the driver refused to stop. Video shows the vehicle striking a curb, accelerating and nearly driving into a yard as it attempted to evade officers.

According to police, the driver's actions posed an immediate danger to others on the road, prompting an officer to deploy a Grappler device that successfully brought the vehicle to a stop.

Officers spent more than 40 minutes communicating with the driver and evaluating multiple options to gain compliance, including a 40 mm less-lethal launcher and pepper balls.

item.title: Apparent road rage driver appears to threaten mom on camera as 3-year-old cries in back seat
item.description: A North Carolina mom says an apparent road rage driver brake-checked her and threatened to kill her as her 3-year-old cried and officials acknowledged a dispatch error.
item.content:encoded:
A mother recorded an apparent road rage encounter on a North Carolina interstate after another driver allegedly cut her off, brake-checked her and repeatedly threatened to kill her while her 3-year-old son cried in the back seat.

Myeka Dunn told FOX8 WGHP she was driving to drop her son off at her mother’s house at about 4:30 p.m. Friday when a dark blue sedan swerved into her lane.

After Dunn honked her horn, the situation escalated rapidly as the driver attempted to cut her off, repeatedly brake-checked her and shouted violent threats, she said.

"They almost hit me, so that's when I honked my horn at them," Dunn said.

WATCH: DRIVER SMIRKS IN MUGSHOT AFTER ALLEGEDLY HITTING GROUP OF CYCLISTS IN CAUGHT-ON-CAMERA ROAD RAGE

Dunn said she pulled out her phone and began recording as the man followed her down the highway.

Video shared online appears to show the man leaning out of his vehicle yelling, "You are going to die! You are going to die!" as Dunn's toddler cries in the background.

The driver then continues, "I could kill you! I could kill you!"

"You know my windows were cracked. He was able to see that my child was in the car," Dunn told the outlet. "He totally disregarded that. He didn't care."

Dunn also called both 911 and the Guilford Metro non-emergency line to report the incident and informed dispatchers she had captured video of the incident but said she was disappointed with the response.

WASHINGTON DRIVER CHASES BOY ON DIRT BIKE DOWN SIDEWALK, GETS HIT WITH MULTIPLE CHARGES

"To know that they're still out there and nothing has been done about it is absolutely frustrating and scary," Dunn said.

Deputy Director of Operations Christine Moore told FOX8 WGHP the dispatcher did not follow protocols.

"Typically, … we enter what we call a ‘be on the lookout’ or a BOLO. And we did. However, we did not enter all of the appropriate information that we should have. … She [the dispatcher] did enter the lookout. She didn’t enter all of the information that was pertinent, including that there was a video involved that the officer may want to see," Moore said.

The Greensboro Police Department said officers issued a be-on-the-lookout alert, or BOLO, after receiving reports of a dark blue sedan swerving through traffic and yelling at other motorists.

NEWLY RELEASED VIDEO SHOWS COPS CUFFING TEEN LINKED TO VIOLENT SEX ASSAULT SCANDAL THAT HAS FAMILIES FUMING

Investigators have since identified the driver involved, though no arrest has been made.

"The victim has been advised how to obtain a warrant on a misdemeanor charge from the Magistrate's Office due to the incident occurring outside the presence of officers," the department said in a statement shared on Facebook.

Dunn also told WRAL News she is in the process of obtaining a misdemeanor warrant against the driver.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Greensboro Police Department for further comment.

item.title: Wisconsin man flies helicopter to Cabela's because the drive was too long
item.description: Dennis Pipping, a 69-year-old Wisconsin pilot, landed his helicopter in a Cabela's parking lot to buy bowhunting supplies, prompting a sheriff's response.
item.content:encoded:
Look, sometimes you just really need to go to Cabela's.

And when the store is 50 miles away, you have two options: get in the car and sit in traffic like a schmuck, or fire up the helicopter and be there in minutes.

Dennis Pipping chose the helicopter.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

The 69-year-old Wisconsin pilot flew from Rosendale to the Cabela’s in Richfield on Saturday evening, landing in a mostly empty section of the store’s parking lot so he could pick up some bowhunting supplies.

Naturally, some busybody saw a helicopter descend outside Cabela’s and called the police.

Washington County sheriff’s deputies arrived to investigate the unusual landing, only to discover there was no emergency, no dramatic getaway and no criminal activity.

Nothing to see here. Just a man who values his time and urgently needed a fresh pack of broadheads.

"So I asked my neighbor friend if he wanted to take a ride to Cabela’s to get some shopping done," Pipping said.

Pipping, who has decades of flying experience, said he called the store before making the approximately 20-minute flight. He also circled the parking lot beforehand to make sure he had enough room to land safely.

When asked why he decided to fly rather than make the roughly 45-minute drive, Pipping responded with a question of his own.

"Why would you drive if you can fly there in a helicopter?" he said.

The man has a point.

OREGON BALLOT MEASURE THAT WOULD HAVE CRIMINALIZED HUNTING AND FISHING FAILS TO QUALIFY FOR VOTE

Pipping said there were no vehicles near the far end of the massive parking lot, allowing him to land, head inside and complete his shopping without incident.

By the time he returned, however, a deputy was waiting to check out the aircraft.

Pipping was properly licensed, had landed safely and complied with applicable Federal Aviation Administration regulations. He was not arrested or cited.

The sheriff’s office ultimately described the incident as a "unique way to make a shopping trip."

And it's even faster than Amazon.
